messages.content: Analyze this sentence.  "Consydre thou myne condicyon; reflecte upon myne fader. Shall I forsake hym, when he is strycken wyth blyndnesse and destytute, to wrastle wyth infirmitie and penurye, when it lyeth wythin my poure to rendre hys latter yeeres fylled wyth comforte and joye?" Each paragraph of your response must end with the same word it started with, separate paragraphs with a newline.

message.content:
This passage is written in a deliberately archaic style of English, using spellings such as 'myne,' 'fader,' 'consydre,' and 'strycken' to evoke the prose of early printed books. This

style immediately signals a literary or dramatic context, perhaps a soliloquy or a moral treatise, in which the speaker addresses the reader directly with the formal second person 'thou.' style

The rhetorical force of the sentence comes from its structure: a series of escalating descriptions of the father's suffering—blindness, destitution, infirmity, and poverty—is followed by the revelation that the speaker has the power to help, making the question of abandonment seem almost inconceivable. The
